title: Comments of Vistra Corp. on PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s 10/29/2025 Waiver Request under ER26-313.

                                   COMMENTS OF VISTRA CORP.

        Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy

Regulatory Commission (“Commission”),1 and the Commission’s October 30, 2025, notice in the

above-captioned docket, Vistra Corp. (“Vistra”) hereby submits these comments on PJM

Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (“PJM”) October 29, 2025 waiver request (“PJM Waiver Request”).2

Vistra supports the requested waiver to restore Susquehanna Nuclear, LLC’s (“Susquehanna”)

148 MW of Capacity Interconnection Rights (“CIRs”) and files these comments out of an

abundance of caution to ensure clarity in the record.

        Susquehanna previously surrendered 148 MW of CIRs because it planned to serve that

amount of load behind-the-meter.3 That new co-located load will instead become Network Load

in front-of-the-meter.4 As a result, the Susquehanna capacity that would otherwise have directly

served the 148 MW co-located load can now be available to the PJM capacity market if the

Commission grants waiver to restore those CIRs. Vistra supports the waiver request and the

restoration of Susquehanna’s previously surrendered CIRs. Vistra agrees that allowing generation

 resources, like Susquehanna, to retain CIRs that were previously committed to a co-located load

can have important benefits for the PJM region.

        However, Vistra wishes to clarify in the record that behind-the-meter co-location

arrangements have equal or better resource adequacy, reliability, and affordability outcomes

compared to front-of-the-meter co-location arrangements.5 Vistra submits this comment out of an

abundance of caution to ensure that certain statements in PJM’s Waiver Request are not taken out

of context. For instance, PJM states that restoring Susquehanna’s 148 MW of CIRs will “benefit

ratepayers and reliability given tightening system conditions” because that capacity will be “made

available to participate in the Base Residual Action (‘BRA’) for the 2027/2028 Delivery Year[.]”).6

Vistra agrees with this statement insofar as it is beneficial to include the 148 MW of CIRs in the

BRA given that the co-located load will become Network Load. However, if the co-located load

were not network load and were instead served behind-the-meter, as previously planned, then the

PJM Reliability Requirement would have been lower because PJM would not have had to include

the 148 MW load or its associated reserve margin. Indeed, removing both the incremental load

and generation from the capacity market would result in the same level of overall resource

adequacy and reliability, with equal or lower capacity market prices for consumers.

        Vistra also wishes to clarify that, contrary to language in PJM’s filing, Susquehanna’s

previously planned behind-the-meter arrangement is not a “novel interconnection configuration.”7

Co-location of load with generation dates back to at least the early implementation of the Public

necessarily unique to co-location and that significant load growth more generally may raise may of the same
concerns.” PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 190 FERC ¶ 61,115, at P 85 (2025).

 Utility Regulatory Policies Act over forty years ago.8 The ongoing litigation with regard to the

Commission’s rejection of the latest amendment to the Susquehanna ISA, filed in Docket No.

ER24-2172, specifically addresses incremental behind-the-meter co-located load and certain non-

conforming ISA language that the Commission found PJM did not adequately justify. Further, the

Commission itself emphasized that the determination in that proceeding was limited to the facts

of that case, and did not prejudice behind-the-meter arrangements or prevent the submission of

other non-conforming interconnection agreements involving such configurations.9

         Vistra asserts that the Commission should promptly grant PJM’s waiver request, but in so

doing, should take care not to inadvertently find that front-of-the-meter co-location arrangements

provide a reliability benefit over behind-the-meter co-location arrangements. Likewise, the

Commission should take care not to inadvertently suggest that there is any question about the

permissibility of behind-the-meter co-location in general. To the extent the Commission seeks to

speak to those issues, there are multiple open proceedings in which it can and should do so, rather

than address such issues in this docket. Moreover, there is sufficient basis for granting the waiver

request here without addressing such issues.
